classification.difficultyReason: Apply the explicitly requested Pythagorean constraint, differentiate the supplied cubic model with a positive constant, test the maximum and recover the depth.

content.prompt: Engineers have determined that the strength $s$ of a rectangular beam varies as the product of the width $w$ and the square of the depth $d$ of the beam, that is, $s=kwd^2$ for some $k>0$.

spec.sourceRegion: Question 25, circular log cross-section below the parts
spec.description: Unshaded circle containing an inscribed rectangle. Its bottom-left to top-right diagonal passes through the marked centre and is labelled 48 cm. The bottom side is labelled w, the right side d, and the bottom-right corner has an internal right-angle mark. Ordinary source grey outlines use house black.
spec.mathematics: The rectangle's diagonal is a diameter of the circle, so w²+d²=48². The schematic aspect ratio supplies no additional measurement.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible; optimised dimensions are not shown.

children.label: a
children.prompt: A particular cylindrical log has a diameter of 48 cm. Use Pythagoras' theorem to show that $s=kw(2304-w^2)$.

answer.worked:
By Pythagoras' theorem,
$$\begin{align*}w^2+d^2&=48^2\\d^2&=2304-w^2.\end{align*}$$
Substitute into $s=kwd^2$, where $k>0$:
$$s=kw(2304-w^2).$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence find the dimensions of the strongest rectangular beam that can be cut from the log.

answer.worked:
For a non-degenerate beam, $0<w<48$.
$$\begin{align*}s&=2304kw-kw^3\\\frac{ds}{dw}&=2304k-3kw^2.\end{align*}$$
At a stationary point,
$$\begin{align*}2304k-3kw^2&=0\\w^2&=768\\w&=16\sqrt3\qquad(w>0).\end{align*}$$
Also,
$$\frac{d^2s}{dw^2}=-6kw.$$
Since $k>0$, $\dfrac{d^2s}{dw^2}<0$ throughout $0<w<48$. Thus strength is maximised at $w=16\sqrt3\text{ cm}$.

Substitute into $d^2=2304-w^2$:
$$\begin{align*}d^2&=2304-(16\sqrt3)^2\\d^2&=1536\\d&=16\sqrt6\qquad(d>0).\end{align*}$$
The dimensions are width $16\sqrt3\text{ cm}$ and depth $16\sqrt6\text{ cm}$.
